document_sections.heading: Executive Summary
document_sections.content: At least 2.2 billion people worldwide are estimated to have vision impairment; for at least 1 billion of them, it was preventable or remains unaddressed. These figures capture only part of the need for eye care: eye conditions can affect anyone, and people who live long enough will experience at least one requiring care. Estimated annual global productivity losses associated with vision impairment are US$ 410.7 billion purchasing power parity, compared with an estimated US$ 24.8 billion gap in funding to address unmet needs. Effective and sometimes highly cost-effective approaches span health promotion, prevention, treatment and rehabilitation. Expanded provision during the past 30 years has accompanied declining age-adjusted blindness from preventable causes and fewer children and adults blinded by vitamin A deficiency, onchocerciasis and trachoma. Nevertheless, services have not kept up with needs driven by demographic, behavioural and lifestyle changes, particularly the growing burden of noncommunicable eye conditions. Eye conditions and vision impairment disproportionately affect LMICs and underserved populations. In many LMICs, practice differs substantially from evidence-based recommendations: essential equipment is often unavailable, particularly in government services, and insurance schemes may exclude eye care medicines and interventions. Costs impede access. Because most eye care in LMICs is delivered in urban secondary or tertiary hospitals, stronger primary-level services and effective referral to higher levels are important. Following resolution WHA73, adopted in November 2020 at the Seventy-third World Health Assembly, WHO developed the PECI with international experts to support evidence-based, cost-effective eye care within universal health coverage. The PECI identifies recommended interventions and implementation resources across health promotion and prevention, screening, diagnosis and monitoring, treatment, and rehabilitation. For each intervention it identifies the relevant life stage, delivery level—community, primary, secondary or tertiary care—and possible connections to programmes and sectors. It is intended to inform national service packages and policies, service delivery planning, and programmes supported by donors and development agencies.

document_sections.heading: Figure 1. Recommended integration of a range of eye care interventions within the health system, across the continuum of care
document_sections.content: The figure places promotion and prevention, screening, clinical examination, treatment and rehabilitation across community and primary, secondary, and tertiary care, connected by referral. Community and primary activities include vision screening and referral, visual acuity and external-eye assessment, spectacles, initial care for eye discomfort or injury, and basic rehabilitation advice or products. Higher levels provide comprehensive examination, retinal screening for high-risk groups, management of common conditions, specialized surgical and nonsurgical care, comprehensive low-vision assessment, assistive-product training, mobility training and visual-skills training. Eye-health education and promotion are recommended at every care level, with particular emphasis on simple counselling and education in community and primary care. The high-risk retinal screening shown refers to preterm and/or low-birth-weight infants at risk of retinopathy of prematurity and people with diabetes at risk of diabetic retinopathy. Community and primary rehabilitation differs in scope from rehabilitation at higher levels. Ready-made reading spectacles can be provided in communities and primary facilities; prescription spectacles for distance refractive error should also be made available as close to people’s homes as feasible.

document_sections.heading: Eye care: global situation
document_sections.content: At least 2.2 billion people worldwide are estimated to have vision impairment, including at least 1 billion whose impairment was preventable or has not yet been addressed. These estimates represent only some of the need for eye care. Eye conditions are universal over a sufficiently long lifetime. In the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017, vision impairment ranked third among impairments by years lived with disability; cited studies also associate eye conditions and impaired vision with substantial losses in well-being. Conservative estimates put annual global productivity losses at approximately US$ 410.7 billion purchasing power parity, versus an estimated US$ 24.8 billion cost gap for addressing unmet vision-impairment needs. Population ageing and growth, together with behavioural and lifestyle factors, are expected to increase conditions capable of impairing vision. More than 800 million people currently have distance or near impairment addressable with appropriate spectacles, while an estimated 100 million have moderate-to-severe distance impairment or blindness correctable through cataract surgery. Presbyopia and cataract arise with ageing; growing evidence suggests lifestyle-related risks will drive projected increases in myopia among younger people. Glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy and complications of myopia are also expected to become more common. Their management requires varied interventions and long-term care, placing pressure on health systems and workforces. On the basis of projected diabetes burden alone, the number needing routine retinal examination for diabetic retinopathy is estimated to rise by 50% by 2040; examination is annual or biennial according to setting.

document_sections.content: The figure presents projected global numbers, in millions, for glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration (any) at successive points from 2016 through 2030. It is adapted from cited systematic reviews and projections.

document_sections.heading: Availability of, and access to, eye care interventions
document_sections.content: Effective approaches across promotion, prevention, treatment and rehabilitation exist, and some are among the most feasible and cost-effective health interventions. Cataract surgery has been identified among a small group of surgical interventions costing less than US$ 200 per disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) averted. During the past 30 years, cataract surgery rates have risen substantially in many LMICs, while large public-health initiatives have substantially reduced childhood and adult blindness caused by vitamin A deficiency, onchocerciasis and trachoma across regions. The proportion of adults impaired or blind from specifically preventable or treatable causes has declined modestly. Services nevertheless lag behind growing need, especially in LMICs. Age-standardized blindness prevalence is 11.1 and 10.7 per 1000 in western and eastern sub-Saharan Africa, respectively, and 10 per 1000 in south-east Asia: more than five times the rate in high-income regions (<2.0 per 1000). Uncorrected near-vision impairment is also most burdensome in LMICs. Underserved groups with a greater burden include rural residents, people with low incomes, women, older people, people with certain disabilities, indigenous populations and ethnic minorities. Evidence-based practice is hindered by shortages of essential equipment and medicines, particularly in parts of the government sector. In a 2019 survey covering all 194 WHO Member States, only 58% reported retinal photocoagulation as generally available in publicly funded care; availability was reported by over 90% of high-income countries but less than 10% of low-income countries. A Nigerian survey found laser access among only approximately 30% of ophthalmologists and a lack of basic diagnostic equipment in 15–20% of clinics. Service costs frequently obstruct access. Among 29 countries completing a WHO eye care service assessment between 2014 and 2016, 59% were low-income or low- to middle-income; more than 20% reported insurance schemes covering no eye care, and several others reported minimal coverage. Most services in LMICs operate from urban secondary or tertiary hospitals, potentially worsening inequity. Eye care therefore needs stronger integration into primary health care and effective referral for timely treatment at secondary and tertiary levels.

document_sections.heading: Universal health coverage and eye care
document_sections.content: The SDGs set priorities agreed by all 193 UN Member States for achievement by 2030. Eye care relates to SDG3 on health and well-being and SDG3.8 on UHC. UHC aims to make needed promotive, preventive, curative and rehabilitative services accessible when and where needed without unaffordable personal payments. Eye care can contribute because unmet need is extensive and effective interventions exist. To address demographic pressures, inequitable access and poor integration, eye care needs to form part of UHC. Equitable access and financial protection require high-priority interventions in service packages financed through prepaid pooled arrangements, particularly for the poorest and neglected groups. Progress involves expanding the priority services in benefit packages, covering a larger share of the population and reducing out-of-pocket spending; countries must decide which populations and interventions to prioritize. In November 2020, the Seventy-third World Health Assembly adopted resolution WHA73 on integrated people-centred eye care and requested WHO guidance supporting evidence-based, cost-effective integration into UHC. Developed with international experts, the PECI supplies intervention and implementation-resource information applicable to most low- and intermediate-resource settings and supports national policy and package decisions.

document_sections.content: The figure represents UHC through three related dimensions: the services included, the population covered and the proportion of direct costs covered. It depicts adding services, extending coverage to people not yet covered, and reducing fees and cost sharing relative to current pooled funds.

document_sections.heading: Methodology
document_sections.content: The PECI methodology was developed with the WHO Guideline Review Committee. Its staged, multi-stakeholder process selected conditions using evidence on causes of vision impairment and blindness, condition prevalence and health-facility data; identified interventions and supporting evidence from CPGs and high-quality systematic reviews through a technical working group; obtained expert agreement on included interventions and their resource requirements; and underwent peer review. Inclusion required evidence of effectiveness judged sufficient in view of recommendation strength and evidence quality, together with practical, realistic implementation in low- and intermediate-resource settings. Annex 1 describes development in more detail, and Annex 2 identifies the guidelines and reviews used.

document_sections.heading: Figure 5. Phases of development of the Package of Eye Care Interventions
document_sections.content: Development proceeded through selection of eye conditions, identification of evidence-based interventions, agreement on interventions and delivery platforms with specification of necessary resources, and peer review.

document_sections.heading: Development and criteria for the selection of eye care interventions for primary care
document_sections.content: A dedicated WHO working group sought low-cost, high-impact, evidence-based eye care interventions and resources deliverable easily, safely and effectively in low-resource primary-care facilities. Intended implementers are primary-level health professionals and allied personnel with health qualifications outside eye care; the model supports task shifting. Development involved reviewing existing WHO materials on primary eye care and primary health care, then obtaining independent input and holding group discussions with primary-eye-care experts. Selection considered whether an intervention addresses common eye conditions causing impaired vision or substantial discomfort; can be delivered safely and effectively, with rare adverse events or minimal side effects, through simple reasoning supported by protocols and brief training; has indications identifiable by basic screening, whether or not diagnosis is definitive; fits routine staff time and roles; and uses inexpensive, locally available equipment or consumables or requires only minimal investment.

document_sections.heading: Scope
document_sections.content: The PECI recommends evidence-based interventions along health promotion and prevention, screening, diagnosis and monitoring, treatment, and rehabilitation. Entries identify the applicable life stage, proposed delivery level—community, primary, secondary or tertiary—and possible programme or sector links. Annexes 3–6 identify equipment, medicines, consumables and assistive technologies needed for implementation. The list is neither exhaustive nor exclusive: it represents interventions supported by high-quality evidence and applicable to most low- and intermediate-resource settings. Future revisions are intended to use emerging evidence and newly collected service-delivery data. Countries differ in health-system maturity, resources and local needs, so the document supports locally appropriate selection and prioritization. Interventions in screening, treatment and rehabilitation designated “essential” were judged by subspecialty expert groups to merit inclusion in national service packages or policies in every country because of condition prevalence or vision-loss risk and a favourable relationship between patient benefit and public-health resources.

document_sections.heading: Figure 6. Integrated eye care at all service delivery levels
document_sections.content: Community eye care is delivered in places such as homes and schools; its boundaries vary by country. Primary eye care is incorporated and coordinated in primary-level facilities by suitably trained workers and allied personnel. Secondary care may be integrated across inpatient and outpatient specialties or provided in dedicated eye facilities, accessed directly, by primary-care referral or through outreach. Tertiary care takes place in specialized hospitals or clinics at the second referral level and above, generally regional or national hospitals, and provides complex subspecialty services with specialized staff and technologies.

document_sections.heading: Box 1. A note on primary care
document_sections.content: Definitions of primary eye care differ among countries, and no single model applies everywhere. Services may be incorporated into primary facilities through training and supervision of existing personnel, or delivered through dedicated fixed or mobile primary-eye-care units. This document concentrates on integration into primary-level facilities in low-resource settings. Beyond the recommended essential interventions, additional assessment, treatment and rehabilitation options labelled “primary plus” can strengthen primary services. These should be considered alongside essential primary care and offered across varied communities and settings to address common needs.

document_sections.heading: Target audience
document_sections.content: The principal users are ministries of health and other ministries planning eye care in low- and middle-income settings. Government providers may use the PECI to plan and deliver services; training institutions to design curricula; researchers to identify evidence gaps and plan research; and donors and development agencies to guide programmes in low- and intermediate-resource settings.

document_sections.heading: Health promotion and prevention
document_sections.content: This section addresses evidence-based promotion, education and clinical and non-clinical prevention in eye care, including opportunities to connect these activities with other programmes and sectors.

document_sections.heading: Health promotion and education
document_sections.content: Promotion, education and counselling seek to build knowledge, motivation and skills so people can act on factors affecting their eye health. Health literacy helps individuals and families, especially underserved groups, adopt healthy behaviours, practise self-care and use services. Historically, eye-health promotion and education have received less attention and investment than treatment. The WHO World report on vision (2019) recommends wider awareness and greater engagement and empowerment of people and communities. Because early identification and timely management can prevent most vision impairment and blindness, people at increased risk—including older adults, people with diabetes and those with a family history of eye conditions—need awareness of regular examinations. Misconceptions such as regarding reduced sight as an inevitable part of ageing also need addressing. Limited eye-health literacy may impede medication adherence and routine review in chronic eye disease. In children and adolescents, spectacle use is often suboptimal, commonly because of stigma and parental misconceptions that spectacles worsen vision.

document_sections.heading: Clinical and non-clinical preventative interventions
document_sections.content: Non-clinical prevention can address myopia, ocular infections and injuries. In children, spending more time outdoors and less time on near work can slow myopia progression and lower the risk of high myopia and its complications. Trauma-prevention awareness campaigns and regulatory or policy action on public and occupational safety can reduce eye injuries. Preventing vitamin A deficiency, measles and rubella through vitamin A supplementation and immunization reduces secondary corneal opacities. After diabetes develops, control of hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia can prevent or delay diabetic retinopathy and its progression. For trachoma-endemic populations, the “SAFE” strategy uses eyelid surgery [S] to reduce continuing visual impairment, antibiotic [A] mass drug administration to lower prevalence, and facial cleanliness [F] and environmental improvement [E] to reduce transmission. Preventive clinical interventions can also target ophthalmia neonatorum and retinopathy of prematurity.

document_sections.heading: Priority areas of health promotion and prevention in the field of eye care
document_sections.content: Table 1 organizes evidence-based promotion and prevention priorities for children, adults and all ages, distinguishing educational and clinical measures and their links to other programmes. Education can take place during routine individual care or through population campaigns. Eye-health promotion and education are recommended across all care levels, with increased attention to straightforward, effective education and counselling in community and primary care. Standalone campaigns are possible, but eye-health messages can also be integrated into occupational health, nutrition, immunization, tobacco cessation and sun-protection programmes. Promotion, education and prevention should complement existing clinical interventions, policies and awareness efforts rather than operate separately. The PECI does not provide guidance on vitamin A supplementation to reduce corneal-ulceration risk or on medical management of diabetic-retinopathy risk factors; it points to other WHO guidance for these subjects. Where vitamin A deficiency is a public-health problem, the document refers readers to WHO maternal and newborn guidance. In trachoma-endemic communities, counselling should also cover appropriate disposal of human faeces to restrict breeding sites for flies transmitting trachoma. Stronger promotion and prevention require personnel able to give simple, effective counselling; eye-care education incorporated into related public campaigns with eye-related outcomes included in evaluation; participation from sectors such as education and labour; and locally appropriate materials, including posters and mHealth tools, for community and primary facilities. Where relevant, regulation or policy can reinforce these measures—for example, workplace protective equipment and restrictions on fireworks, minimum outdoor time during school, or taxation of harmful products such as tobacco.

document_sections.heading: Box 2. Case study: An initiative to delay the onset and progression of myopia in Singapore: using public education awareness and vision screening*
document_sections.content: Singapore’s School Health Service implemented the National Myopia Prevention Programme through collaboration among ministries, professional bodies, academic institutions and researchers. Beginning in 2002, it combined public education intended to delay childhood myopia with screening for early detection and management; routine annual school screening had begun in 1996. The programme later included preschool children as young as 5 years of age. Its evidence-based messages encouraged outdoor activity and less near work, including reading, writing and electronic-device use. Activities addressed children, parents, teachers and the public through child-friendly performances and a mobile bus, teacher training, family counselling and public events, mass media, and online information. An analysis of students at 12 primary and 12 secondary schools between 2004 and 2015 found a statistically significant decline in myopia prevalence among primary-school students only, from 37.7% to 31.6%. This result is attributed to the cited analysis of the programme.

Topics include childhood myopia prevention, spectacle adherence, nutrition and immunization, oxygen management in preterm infants, neonatal eye-infection prophylaxis, diabetic-retinopathy risk control, lifestyle risks, acute angle-closure glaucoma awareness, regular examinations, treatment adherence, injury prevention and limiting the spread of eye infections.

document_sections.heading: Screening of high-risk populations
document_sections.content: This section considers screening at important life stages and in populations at increased risk.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Vision impairment may develop gradually and remain unnoticed, particularly in adults; delayed diagnosis and treatment can have serious, lasting consequences throughout life. Some conditions, including diabetic retinopathy, can also be asymptomatic early on. Screening is therefore important for early identification of relevant conditions in high-risk groups and of vision impairment at key life stages.

document_sections.heading: Neonatal period
document_sections.content: Screening during the neonatal period, followed when necessary by prompt interventions including surgery, can protect visual development in children born with conditions such as congenital cataract, congenital glaucoma or retinoblastoma. WHO postnatal-care recommendations call for an external-eye examination and red-reflex test for every infant at birth or at the first well-baby-clinic contact, with prompt or urgent eye-care referral after a positive screen. More preterm births and improved survival have made retinopathy of prematurity a leading cause of childhood blindness in many middle-income countries and an emerging concern in several African countries. This increases the need for high-quality neonatal care, integrated prevention, systematic screening of preterm and/or low-birth-weight infants, timely referral for indicated treatment, and long-term follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Children and adolescents
document_sections.content: Refractive error, particularly myopia, is expected to affect substantially more children and adolescents in coming decades. A cited global systematic review and meta-analysis projects 200 million additional children and adolescents with myopia between 2000 and 2050. Because sight matters for education and refractive error is frequent at preschool and school ages, preschool vision screening and screening within school-health services, followed promptly by correction or other care such as amblyopia management, can mitigate unaddressed impairment. School-based vision and external-eye assessment, spectacle provision and referral commonly require coordination with eye-care professionals at other levels and cooperation between health and education ministries. Where no school-health programme exists, local epidemiology, including refractive-error prevalence, should guide whether separate school screening is warranted.

document_sections.heading: Older adults
document_sections.content: Near- and distance-vision impairment are substantially more prevalent at older ages. An estimated 80% of distance-vision impairment and blindness and two-thirds of near-vision impairment occur at age 50 years or older. Although screening visual acuity across the general population is not considered cost-effective in most settings, older adults need readily accessible, active visual-acuity assessment followed by appropriate intervention. General practitioners, primary-level doctors and community health workers can perform such assessments. WHO guidance on integrated care for older people recommends primary-care visual-acuity assessment for those aged ≥60 years and timely access to comprehensive eye care.

document_sections.heading: People with diabetes
document_sections.content: The number of people with diabetes has increased across countries during the past 30 years alongside lifestyle changes. Diabetic retinopathy is the most common diabetic microvascular complication and a leading preventable cause of vision impairment and blindness. If existing trends persist, a cited estimate projects a 1.2-fold rise in affected people, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030. Most associated vision impairment can be avoided through risk-factor control, early identification and timely treatment. Many national and international professional societies have long endorsed systematic retinal screening of people with diabetes to detect vision-threatening disease, annually or biennially according to setting, followed by treatment when needed. Approaches include ophthalmoscopy by trained eye-care staff and retinal imaging interpreted locally or centrally through telemedicine. Lower-cost retinal cameras and artificial-intelligence approaches may improve access and quality closer to home.

document_sections.heading: Box 3. Long-term impact of retinal screening on diabetes-related visual impairment in the working-age population: the English National Screening Programme (62)
document_sections.content: England established systematic diabetic-retinopathy screening in 2003 and invites everyone with diabetes aged ≥12 years to annual eye screening, with attendance reminders. Since 2008, annual coverage has been near comprehensive (>80%). Trained screeners measure visual acuity, dilate pupils and obtain two-field retinal photographs; images are transferred for central grading by specially trained nonphysician technicians. Screeners and graders must hold a minimum qualification, while graders complete monthly image tests against a reference grade; the service also uses audit and internal and external quality assurance. Reported sensitivity and specificity for detecting diabetic retinopathy and sight-threatening disease, defined here as moderate disease or worse, have been robust. Sight-threatening findings prompt timely ophthalmology referral, and poor-quality images prompt slit-lamp assessment of retinal status. During 2015–16, the programme screened 2 144 007 people with diabetes, representing 83% coverage. A review of England’s blindness registry after 7 years of screening for treatable disease found diabetic retinopathy was no longer the leading cause of blindness among working-age people. The document presents this programme experience as compelling evidence that systematic screening combined with timely treatment can reduce impairment and blindness.

document_sections.heading: Priority screening interventions in the field of eye care
document_sections.content: Table 2 presents screening priorities for critical life stages and high-risk groups across resource settings, aiming at timely detection of eye conditions and vision impairment. In its care-level columns, 1, 2 and 3 denote primary, secondary and tertiary care, and an “x” denotes a proposed delivery level. Unless otherwise specified, the document defines Neonatal as up to 4 weeks of birth; Early childhood as 28 days to 4 years; Later childhood as 5–9 years; Early adolescence as 10–14 years; Later adolescence/ early youth as 15–19 years; Later youth as 20–24 years; Early adulthood as 25–49 years; Middle adulthood as 50–64 years; and Later adulthood as 65 years and above. Screening infants at risk of retinopathy of prematurity starts a few weeks after birth according to local evidence-based criteria. Although uncommon in most low- and intermediate-resource settings, primary-level diabetic-retinopathy screening by trained non-ophthalmic technicians, with local or remote interpretation, could reach more people. For older adults, the priority is accessible, active visual-acuity assessment followed by suitable care; evidence does not currently support standalone vision-screening programmes for adult populations.

document_sections.heading: Table 2. Priority areas for screening in the field of eye care, stratified by critical stages of the life-course and high-risk populations
document_sections.content: The table distinguishes general-population screening of newborns, preschool and school-age children, and older adults from targeted retinal screening of preterm and/or low-birth-weight infants and people with diabetes. It records the relevant life stage, whether an intervention is essential, proposed care levels, referral and programme links.

document_sections.heading: Clinical examinations for diagnosis and monitoring
document_sections.content: This section identifies essential examinations used for general assessment, diagnosis and monitoring across priority eye conditions.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Early detection followed by timely, appropriate intervention can lessen the effects of many eye conditions and vision impairment throughout life. Community and primary facilities are often the first contact for ocular problems; with adequate resources, they can address needs locally and promptly while improving the efficiency of secondary and tertiary care. Stronger services require funding, appropriate training and a sustainable workforce, coordination across services and sectors, and planned referral systems. Essential community and primary examinations include vision testing at critical life stages and for visual complaints, plus external assessment of the eye and surrounding structures for abnormalities in shape, colour, size, position, direction or lid closure, with timely referral as needed. Annexes 7 and 8 address interventions and resources suitable for low-resource primary facilities. Where health systems mature or resources permit, primary-level examination and intervention should expand through “primary plus”. Given population needs, refractive and optical services and diabetic-retinopathy screening are recommended as priorities at primary facilities or as near to them as possible. Secondary services diagnose and manage both sight-threatening and other common conditions; comprehensive examinations should therefore be available at secondary and tertiary levels, supported by investment in professionals and equipment.

document_sections.heading: Essential clinical examinations for diagnosis and monitoring of eye conditions
document_sections.content: Table 3 assigns recommended essential diagnostic and monitoring examinations to care levels; Annex 3 specifies associated equipment and consumables. Many examinations—including visual acuity testing, slit-lamp examination and ophthalmoscopy—serve multiple conditions, whereas others, such as corneal topography, are condition-specific. The primary-care assessments require additional suitable workforce training and incorporation into future curricula. WHO plans further training materials with follow-up and referral algorithms. External-eye torchlight examination assesses the eye and surrounding structures for shape, colour, size, position, direction and lid closure. Binocular-vision assessment encompasses stereoacuity, ocular motility, fusion and prism testing. Dry-eye assessment includes tear-meniscus height, tear-film break-up time, ocular-surface staining and Schirmer’s test. Functional assessment also addresses vision for learning, occupational needs and daily activities, with parent or caregiver input. OCT is considered the gold standard for diagnosis and monitoring of treatment regimens across several retinal disorders, but costs currently limit access in many low- and middle-income countries. Emerging developments may lower device costs. At tertiary level, additional OCT glaucoma and anterior-segment modules are desirable.

document_sections.heading: Table 3. Recommended essential interventions, at each level of care, for the diagnosis and monitoring of eye conditions and vision impairment
document_sections.content: The table sets out which clinical examinations are recommended at community, primary, secondary and tertiary levels. It distinguishes basic community and primary assessments from broader specialist testing and marks selected expanded primary services as “plus”.

document_sections.heading: Treatment
document_sections.content: This section addresses evidence-based surgical and nonsurgical interventions for priority eye conditions.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: After diagnosis, a doctor or suitably trained health professional may prescribe medication, a nonsurgical intervention, surgery or a combination. Treatment can seek cure, relieve symptoms, and prevent or slow deterioration toward vision impairment. Spectacles and cataract surgery address the two leading global causes of impaired vision—uncorrected refractive error and unoperated cataract—and rank among highly cost-effective health interventions. In May 2021, the Seventy-fourth World Health Assembly endorsed 2030 targets of a 40% increase in effective refractive-error coverage and a 30% increase in effective cataract-surgery coverage to encourage wider, good-quality care. Spectacles or contact lenses can fully correct refractive-error-related reduced vision; laser surgery can correct it in adulthood. Spectacles are noninvasive assistive products included in the WHO Priority Assistive Products List. In many LMICs they are regarded as cosmetic rather than medical products, while refractive and optical services are often private, creating problems of access, affordability and quality. Further obstacles include shortages of qualified optometrists and optical technicians, limited government oversight and clinical regulation, predominantly urban service points, and low awareness or acceptance. Wider spectacle access requires action across sectors to increase demand and screening and supply points and to accelerate affordable products. WHO’s planned 2022 SPECS Initiative aims to support equitable provision, professional capacity, public education, lower costs, and stronger research and surveillance. Cataract surgery removes the clouded lens and implants an artificial intraocular lens. The three approaches described are phacoemulsification, manual SICS and ECCE. Phacoemulsification predominates in high-income settings; SICS and ECCE remain common where resources are more limited because phacoemulsification equipment and consumables cost more. ECCE has been demonstrated safe and effective, but evidence indicates longer recovery and worse uncorrected postoperative vision than with phacoemulsification or SICS. The cited literature suggests phacoemulsification and SICS have comparable safety and efficacy. Increased cataract-surgery rates in many LICs and LMICs during the past two decades have produced only modest reductions in the global proportion impaired or blind because of cataract, alongside demographic changes. In some settings, barriers including culture, convenience, cost and poor access have led people to harmful traditional procedures. Wider surgical coverage is challenged by patient costs, reaching underserved groups and maintaining quality; cited evidence suggests postoperative vision results can be suboptimal. Unlike the relatively short course of cataract treatment, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, complications of high myopia and retinopathy of prematurity often require prolonged follow-up. Glaucoma management may combine medicines, laser and surgery to reduce further progression. Screening followed by laser or other treatment can lower vision-loss risk in diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity. Continuous or intermittent intraocular anti-VEGF injections are available for neovascular age-related macular degeneration only and for myopic macular degeneration. Timely treatment, including surgery, can prevent delayed visual development in children with conditions such as congenital cataract, congenital glaucoma, retinoblastoma and amblyopia. Dry eye, conjunctivitis and blepharitis commonly call for symptom relief even though they do not typically impair vision. Advanced pterygium affecting vision often requires surgery. Prompt surgical and nonsurgical care for blunt trauma, corneal abrasions, foreign bodies, penetrating injuries and burns is important to preserve vision. Conditions not usually causing impairment also warrant service-planning attention because they frequently prompt care-seeking.

document_sections.heading: Priority, evidence-based, treatment interventions in the field of eye care
document_sections.content: Table 4 sets out priority surgical and nonsurgical interventions for the selected conditions. Annexes 4 and 5 specify related equipment, consumables and medicines. School-based spectacle provision may require coordination with professionals at other levels for examinations, refraction or dispensing. People with clinically significant anisometropia and astigmatism require custom-made reading spectacles. Three adult cataract operations are listed separately because resource needs and costs differ substantially; pediatric cataract surgery is separate because its personnel and equipment needs differ from adult surgery. The availability, cost-effectiveness and workforce of each country inform delivery of certain glaucoma procedures. The scope of selected primary-level interventions differs from their scope at higher levels. Although intravitreal anti-VEGF is considered the gold standard for treating several retinal disorders, cost currently restricts its availability in many low- and middle-income countries; emerging developments may reduce treatment costs.

document_sections.heading: Table 4. Priority non-surgical and surgical interventions for the priority eye conditions
document_sections.content: The table groups priority interventions by refractive error, amblyopia and strabismus, cataract, glaucoma, anterior-segment and adnexal conditions, uveitis, vitreoretinal disease, ocular cancer and general postoperative or surgical needs. For each, it identifies the intended life stage, whether it is designated essential or surgical, proposed delivery levels, a brief clinical purpose and applicable programme links.

document_sections.heading: Corneal transplantation
document_sections.content: Corneal opacities remain a leading cause of blindness in LMICs. Although the PECI includes transplantation, many countries lack enough donor tissue because donation, eye banking and transplantation programmes are absent or inadequate. One cited study estimates only 1 donated cornea worldwide for every 70 needed. Out-of-pocket tissue and care costs are additional barriers. Sustainable corneal banking requires better information on donation rates and population needs, clear donation and transplantation policies and legislation, and supportive governance. Prevention is also important because leading transplant indications, including ocular trauma and corneal infection, can be avoided.

document_sections.heading: Emerging treatment interventions
document_sections.content: A growing number of promising treatments did not satisfy PECI inclusion criteria when the package was developed. Examples include emerging approaches to prevention and treatment of dry eye disease and management of myopia. Future work is intended to refine and expand the PECI using new evidence and service-delivery data.

document_sections.heading: Rehabilitation
document_sections.content: This section introduces priority evidence-based vision rehabilitation interventions.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: UHC encompasses rehabilitation as well as other health needs. For people with impaired vision or blindness, rehabilitation seeks better everyday functioning by making the most of remaining vision and addressing the social, psychological, emotional and economic consequences through practical adaptations. The WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health model can help describe effects on daily activities, education, work and social participation. Approximately 60 million adults worldwide are estimated to have irreversible moderate or severe distance-vision impairment or blindness requiring rehabilitation. In adults, the principal relevant causes include glaucoma, macular disease, corneal opacities and diabetic retinopathy; in children and young adults they include congenital and genetic conditions, acquired conditions and cerebral vision impairment. Available interventions include optical, non-optical and electronic assistive products, environmental changes such as improved lighting, and orientation and mobility training. These measures can improve functioning and participation in community life, education and employment. Despite this, evidence suggests rehabilitation coverage is poor or absent in most LMICs. Demographic change and increasing irreversible impairment will raise demand further. Existing services commonly sit in tertiary public or private facilities or depend on nongovernmental organizations for provision and funding, creating access and sustainability concerns.

document_sections.heading: Priority, evidence-based, vision rehabilitation interventions
document_sections.content: Table 5 identifies priority vision rehabilitation interventions, and Annex 6 specifies the assistive products and consumables they require. Rehabilitation must reflect each person’s needs and priorities because eye conditions can affect different aspects of visual function. The interventions include psychological support; optical, non-optical and electronic assistive products; advice on adapting living environments; orientation and mobility training; and visual skills training. Provision or replacement of assistive products through school health or community-based rehabilitation programmes requires coordination with, and referral to, trained eye care professionals at higher care levels for examination, diagnosis, prescription and instruction in product use. Wider access requires incorporating vision rehabilitation into health-sector planning, relevant health programmes and education. Public policy and adequately resourced implementation plans must also support accessible environments; examples for public spaces include tactile paving before crossings, audible crossing signals and tactile signs. Putting these interventions into practice requires appropriate training materials for community and primary-care workers and support for educational settings. WHO is developing a Basic Rehabilitation Package to support delivery of rehabilitation, including vision rehabilitation, in primary-level facilities.

document_sections.heading: Box 4. An integrated low-vision rehabilitation service: a case example from Sri Lanka*
document_sections.content: Before 2008, Sri Lanka had three low-vision clinics serving the country, all in tertiary hospitals. Its first national eye care plan, developed in 2007, incorporated low vision and established links with education, rehabilitation and social services. With Ministry of Health and international nongovernmental support, service strengthening began in 2008. Existing tertiary clinics first developed capacity for visual skills training, orientation and mobility training, and counselling. Subsequently, 10 secondary-level clinics were established in district hospitals with referral links to the three tertiary clinics. Staff from existing eye units were trained to assess low vision comprehensively, prescribe and dispense assistive products, and teach their use; people with complex needs were referred to the nearest tertiary clinic. Access increased, and within two years of implementation nearly 8000 people with vision impairment received rehabilitation; 10% were children. The account describes this as a small share of those needing care in Sri Lanka, but a five-fold increase in service users compared with the previous three years.

document_sections.heading: Implementation strategy
document_sections.content: The section sets out a general approach to implementing PECI and considerations for practical national decisions.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: PECI specifies recommended evidence-based eye care interventions, their material requirements, appropriate community-to-tertiary delivery levels and possible links with other programmes or sectors. The interventions address most eye conditions that substantially affect well-being. Recommendations were developed with LICs and LMICs in mind. Although its priority lists are not exclusive, PECI can inform national policy, strategic planning and integrated service delivery. Each country should devise an implementation plan suited to its needs, epidemiology, health-system rules, infrastructure, workforce, financing and patient affordability.

document_sections.heading: The PECI in the context of the WHO Eye care in health systems: Guide for action
document_sections.content: WHO’s Eye care in health systems: Guide for action describes four phases for integrated people-centred eye care: Phase 1 assesses the situation; Phase 2 develops an eye care strategic plan and monitoring framework; Phase 3 implements the plan; and Phase 4 establishes evaluation and review. WHO recommends a government-led national eye care sector plan involving relevant programmes and sectors, aligned with broader health-sector planning and funding, accompanied by a monitoring framework and revised every four to five years or when necessary. Before planning, WHO recommends the Eye Care Situation Analysis Tool (ECSAT) to identify the sector’s situation and priorities for Phase 1. ECSAT findings should inform Phase 2 goals, objectives and activities. WHO recommends PECI to guide Phase 3 operational planning and budgeting at every health-system level. PECI is also included in WHO’s UHC compendium, which adds workforce requirements and estimated average implementation time for interventions. A future linked tool is intended to support planning, costing, impact analysis, budgeting and financing, including estimates of resource needs, annual costs, health impact and available funding. These resources are intended to help LMICs choose cost-effective actions appropriate to national circumstances.

document_sections.heading: Annex 1. Development process for the Package of Eye Care Interventions
document_sections.content: The WHO Vision and Eye Care Programme coordinated and developed PECI, with methodological and evidence expertise from Cochrane Eyes and Vision. A technical advisory group representing public health, academic and clinical expertise across all six WHO regions contributed throughout development. Eye care experts helped identify evidence, select interventions and define resource needs. In total, 114 public health, academic and clinical professionals from 45 countries contributed.

document_sections.heading: Stages of development of the Package of Eye Care Interventions
document_sections.content: Stage 1 selected conditions using evidence about causes of visual impairment and blindness, condition prevalence and health-facility data, followed by technical advisory group consensus. Vision rehabilitation interventions were considered as well. The scope includes conditions that do not usually impair vision, such as dry eye disease, conjunctivitis, pterygium and blepharitis, because they can be painful or troublesome, substantially affect well-being, frequently prompt care-seeking and create financial burden. Table A1.1 lists the selected conditions without ranking their priority. It groups clinically distinct ocular-surface, eyelid and lacrimal conditions to account for differing treatments and facilitate evidence identification.

document_sections.heading: Stage 2: Identification of evidence-based interventions
document_sections.content: Stage 2 identified and selected clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) and extracted their evidence-based eye care recommendations for subspecialty groups to consider during Stage 3. Figure A1.2 depicts the sequence of searching, screening, quality appraisal, guideline selection and recommendation extraction.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes of the systematic literature search, guideline screening, and quality appraisal
document_sections.content: Separate systematic searches, screening and quality appraisals for refractive error and vision rehabilitation were undertaken in 2019. Following that experience and consideration of feasibility, a single search in 2020 covered the other selected conditions. Selected guideline databases and professional-association websites were also searched manually. Two WHO Vision Programme members centrally screened titles and abstracts and applied exclusion criteria. A technical working group of 33 experts screened full texts and appraised CPG quality by condition. Figures A1.3–A1.5 show the selection flows. For refractive error, the search returned n = 1563 records; n = 1515 were excluded after title and abstract screening, n = 48 full texts were assessed, n = 36 were excluded after full-text and quality assessment, and n =12 CPGs were identified. For vision rehabilitation, n = 1502 records yielded n = 26 assessed full texts after n = 1476 initial exclusions; n = 24 were subsequently excluded and n = 2 CPGs were identified. For the remaining conditions, n = 3778 records yielded n = 469 assessed full texts after n = 3309 initial exclusions; n = 323 were excluded after full-text and quality assessment, and n = 96 CPGs passed appraisal. Systematic reviews supplemented CPG evidence particularly when selected high-quality guidelines disagreed about an intervention or relied on evidence older than 10 years. Data were extracted from 44 systematic reviews.

document_sections.heading: Data extraction and preparation
document_sections.content: Recommendations from selected CPGs and systematic reviews were classified as assessment, health promotion, prevention or treatment. Extracted information also covered the intervention target, setting, dosage or frequency, recommendation strength and quality of supporting evidence. Subspecialty development groups received these findings and the selected full-text publications to inform intervention selection.

document_sections.heading: Stage 3: Selection of interventions and defining the resource requirements
document_sections.content: Working groups for anterior segment, glaucoma, pediatric care, vitreoretinal disorders, refractive error and vision rehabilitation used an initial online survey, virtual discussions and independent written feedback to reach agreement on interventions for PECI and define delivery platforms, workforce, time, equipment, medicines, consumables and assistive technologies. Inclusion required evidence of effectiveness judged sufficient in light of recommendation strength and evidence quality, together with feasible implementation in low- and intermediate-resource settings.

document_sections.heading: Annex 3. Equipment and consumable requirements for eye care examinations, by level of care
document_sections.content: The annex lists equipment and consumables for eye examinations across community and primary care, primary plus, and secondary and tertiary care. Its examinations encompass visual acuity, external-eye assessment, refraction, visual function, intraocular pressure, anterior-segment and retinal evaluation, imaging and functional vision. Some listed supplies are interchangeable options according to preferences, resources or geographical availability; secondary and tertiary lists add to lower-level requirements. OCT is described as the gold standard for diagnosing and monitoring treatment regimens for various retinal disorders, but cost limits its availability in many low- and middle-income countries. Developments may lower device costs. Additional OCT capabilities for glaucoma and the anterior segment are desirable at tertiary level.

document_sections.heading: Annex 4. An overview of the equipment and consumable requirements for treatment interventions
document_sections.content: The annex maps non-surgical and surgical treatment interventions to community, Primary (1), Secondary (2) and Tertiary (3) delivery and their equipment and consumables; Primary (1) includes Primary plus. Its non-surgical entries cover spectacles, amblyopia patching, selected laser procedures, chemical-exposure irrigation, corneal-injury care, keratoconus contact lenses, punctal occlusion, intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy and retinal photocoagulation. Surgical entries cover strabismus, cataract, glaucoma, eyelid, lacrimal, corneal and vitreoretinal procedures, retinopathy of prematurity, retinoblastoma, postoperative infection or inflammation, and evisceration or enucleation. School-health spectacle provision can involve referral to trained professionals for refraction or dispensing. Retinoblastoma care requires a multidisciplinary approach. The subsequent lists detail surgical supplies; some items represent interchangeable options depending on preferences, available resources or geographical availability.

document_sections.heading: 1. Anaesthesia equipment and consumables
document_sections.content: The table specifies equipment and consumables considered essential across anaesthetic procedures, including resuscitation, intravenous access, pulse oximetry and syringes. It separately lists operating-table, oxygen, suction, anaesthesia-system, mask and airway requirements for paediatric anaesthesia.

document_sections.heading: 2. Operating theatre equipment and consumables
document_sections.content: The operating-theatre tables enumerate general protective and sterile supplies, sutures, gloves, needles and syringes, dressings, cautery, sterilization, microscopes, lighting, furniture and cryotherapy equipment needed for the listed surgical interventions.

document_sections.heading: 3. Cataract equipment (general) and consumables
document_sections.content: This table lists general cataract-surgery instruments and supplies by category: forceps, needle holders, blades, scissors, cannulas, intraocular lenses and other operative materials. It identifies 1 piece acrysof IOL as preferred for pediatric cases and identifies hydrophobic acrylic IOL as an option if available.

document_sections.heading: 4. Cataract equipment (SICS)
document_sections.content: Additional equipment for SICS, beyond general cataract equipment and consumables, comprises specified keratomes, a reusable handle for single-use knives and other incision knives.

document_sections.heading: 5. Cataract equipment (Phaco)
document_sections.content: The table supplements general cataract resources with phacoemulsification and anterior-vitrectomy equipment, irrigation and aspiration components, surgical knives and instruments, and a foldable hydrophilic lens with insertion supplies.

document_sections.heading: 6. Vitreoretinal equipment and consumables
document_sections.content: The annex lists viewing systems, vitrectomy equipment, forceps, needle holders, scissors, blades, cannulas, illumination and retinal-surgery instruments, together with consumables for procedures such as tamponade and tissue manipulation.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 Laser equipment (pan retinal, photocoagulation, focal, grid)
document_sections.content: The equipment listed for retinal laser procedures includes a photocoagulator, an endophotocoagulation probe, a vitrectomy lens and retinal lasers specified as Green laser: -532 nm and 810 nm infrared or diode laser.

document_sections.heading: 7. Glaucoma equipment and consumables
document_sections.content: The glaucoma lists specify specula, needle holders, scissors, forceps, cannulas, blades and other surgical supplies, including trabeculotomy instruments, drainage devices, sponges for antifibrotic agents and sterile fluids.

document_sections.heading: 8. Corneal equipment and consumables
document_sections.content: The table describes a corneal suture set and general equipment, needle holders, scissors, forceps, cannulas, blades and other supplies for corneal procedures.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Keratoplasty (penetrating and deep) equipment
document_sections.content: Separate lists specify trephination, fixation, marking and tissue-handling instruments for penetrating keratoplasty, and dissection, air-injection and graft-handling instruments for deep keratoplasty.

document_sections.heading: 9. Eyelid equipment
document_sections.content: The eyelid equipment list includes forceps, clamps, lid plates, scissors and a lid retractor for eyelid procedures.

document_sections.heading: 10. Strabismus equipment and consumables
document_sections.content: The table identifies a speculum, scissors, forceps, extraocular-muscle sutures, an eyelid retractor and hooks for strabismus surgery.

document_sections.heading: 11. Enucleation and evisceration equipment and consumables
document_sections.content: In addition to eyelid and corneal equipment, the table lists instruments for enucleation and evisceration, orbital implants and a conformer.

document_sections.heading: 12. Lacrimal equipment and consumables
document_sections.content: The lacrimal list supplements eyelid and corneal equipment with syringes, lacrimal dilators, Bowman probes and a lacrimal cannula.

document_sections.heading: Annex 5. List of medicines for the Package of Eye Care Interventions
document_sections.content: The annex lists medicines and selected consumables against seven areas: A, refractive error; B, vision rehabilitation; C, cataract; D, glaucoma; E, pediatrics; F, vitreoretina; and G, anterior segment and adnexa. Its categories include dilating and cycloplegic preparations, local and general anaesthetic preparations, antibiotics, antivirals, topical antifungals, drugs for Acanthamoeba keratitis, steroids, antibiotic–steroid combinations, lubricants, glaucoma preparations, age-adjusted retinoblastoma chemotherapy, anti-VEGF drugs, immunosuppressants, systemic biological agents, disinfectants and consumables. The WHO EML column identifies listed drugs also appearing in the World Health Organization Model List of Essential Medicines; it does not constitute a condition-specific prescribing regimen.

document_sections.heading: Annex 6. Assistive product requirements for the vision rehabilitation interventions
document_sections.content: The table identifies optical, non-optical and electronic assistive products, along with products for daily living and mobility, required for rehabilitation interventions. It indicates which items also appear on the World Health Organization Priority Assistive Products List. WHO specifications are available for several of the products.

document_sections.heading: Annex 7. Recommended eye care interventions/resources that can be easily, safely and effectively delivered at primary-level health facilities in low-resource settings
document_sections.content: The annex defines a low-cost, high-impact primary eye care package intended for safe and effective delivery in low-resource primary-level facilities, together with minimum equipment and consumables. Its intervention list is organized by health-service type and life-course. Health education and counselling can address nutrition and immunization, myopia prevention and spectacle adherence, diabetic retinopathy risk factors, behavioural eye-health risks, regular eye examinations, infection prevention and injury prevention. Screening includes neonatal assessment for congenital or acquired conditions and infections, preferably within 72 hrs of birth, and vision and general eye-health assessment for pre-school children aged 3–5 years, school-age children aged 5–18 years, older adults and people with diabetes of all ages; indicated cases require timely referral. Treatment includes assessing near vision and providing readymade reading spectacles when indicated to adults aged 40 years and over. Red eye or abnormal lashes may receive treatment or first aid, follow-up advice and timely referral if improvement is limited or absent; vision loss, eye swelling or a growth on the eyeball requires immediate counselling and referral. Eye injuries, including blunt injury, corneal abrasion, foreign body, sharp or penetrating injury and burns, require immediate first aid and urgent referral. Rehabilitation options include advice on safer and more accessible living environments, assistive products when available, and referral or delivery of psychological support related to vision loss. Cases beyond primary-care capacity require referral under the country’s established system. General eye assessment examines the eye and surrounding structures for abnormalities of shape, colour, size, position, direction and lid closure.

document_sections.heading: Annex 8. Minimum essential equipment and consumables, medicines and deliverable health products for integration of eye care into primary care facilities
document_sections.content: The annex lists essential primary-care examination and first-aid equipment, including recording supplies, near- and distance-vision charts, measuring aids, a pinhole, light, eye shield, gauze, cotton buds, irrigation equipment and personal protective equipment. Epilating forceps are listed as desirable in trachoma-endemic areas. Essential medicine categories include irrigation fluid, topical antibiotics, topical lubricants, vitamin A preparations, topical anaesthetic and tetanus toxoid; the table provides their individual formulations and strengths. Essential deliverable products include readymade reading spectacles in powers +1.50, +2.00, +2.50 and +3.00, referral forms and eye-health educational materials. Assistive products and rehabilitation promotional materials are listed as desirable. For guidance on vitamin A supplementation in infants and children 6–59 months of age, the annex refers to a separate WHO guideline.
